methodological_questions: Can the teammate with the closest pre-absence initiation profile be identified as the largest gainer in the absent player's primary play types?
How is 'closest profile' defined, and does the (or most minutes / initiations / same-position minutes) alternative change the test?
What sample size and exposure are needed for absence-based usage redistribution tests?
How should regression to the mean and selection of absence spells be handled?
Which label and leakage risks arise when play-type initiation is derived from play-by-play outcomes?
evidence_establishes: The retrieval call returned no records, so no prior project study of this question, its sample-size limits, or its failed approaches is available in this setting.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether any earlier project analysis tested absence-based usage redistribution.
Whether the closest-profile teammate has ever been shown to be the largest gainer.
Whether 11 cases are sufficient for any such ranking claim.
Any effect size, base rate, or reliability estimate for play-type initiation measures.
own_inferences: The question is a ranking claim (the top-ranked teammate by similarity is the top gainer), which requires many independent absence cases to evaluate. With 11 cases, each contributing one absent player's reorganization, the top-gainer hit rate has very little resolution.
The 148 spells are nested within 11 cases and are not independent, so the effective sample size is closer to 11 than 148.

The disjunctive definition of 'closest profile' (initiation profile, most minutes, initiations, or same-position minutes) creates a forking-paths problem: the test could be run on whichever definition works.

Most-minutes and same-position teammates are mechanically likely to absorb usage because they receive more opportunities, so a positive result could reflect opportunity rather than profile similarity.
Play-type initiation and points are derived from the same play-by-play outcomes used to define gains, so gains and profile features can share labels, creating circularity.
Teammates are often selected as the largest gainer after a large absent-player share, which inflates apparent gains through regression to the mean.
uncertainties: Exact cell counts per absent player and play type, and how many teammates qualify per case.
Whether 2025-26 playoff data (partial before 2026-06-21) should be excluded.
How many absences are long versus short, and whether spell boundaries are clean from rotation intervals.
Reliability of play-type classification from action type and sub-type fields.
Whether any records were absent from retrieval because the setting has no earlier project work, rather than because none exists.

historical_effect.explanation: No records were returned, so the decision rests only on the task statement, the data description, and general methodological reasoning. The absence of history neither supports nor rules out the question.

blocking_constraints.text: With 11 absence cases, a top-gainer ranking test has very low power; spells within a case are not independent.
Initiation and gain labels are both derived from play-by-play outcomes, so profile and gain measures can be circular.
Primary play-type cells for the absent player and candidate teammates may be too sparse per case to measure gains reliably.

prior_work.summary: No earlier work was retrieved, so it is unknown whether this question has been answered. No prior study is relied on.

risks.text: 11 cases give very little power to test which teammate is the largest gainer; 148 spells overstate the effective sample.
Choosing absences or top gainers after observing large usage shifts inflates apparent redistribution through regression to the mean.
Minutes, same-position status, and role changes (starters, rotation changes) drive both profile similarity and usage gains.
Play-type gains and initiation profiles are both computed from the same play-by-play outcomes, creating circularity.
If profile or minutes are measured over windows that include the absence or post-absence period, the predictor is contaminated by the outcome.
The disjunctive definition of closest profile (four alternatives) and several play types allow many comparisons, raising false-positive risk.
Play-type classification from action and sub-type fields and per-spell counts may be noisy, weakening both profile and gain measures.
Small per-player, per-play-type counts make the gain estimates unstable.
Team context, roster changes, and season-to-season style shifts across 2022-23 to 2025-26 may alter usage independently of absence.
Attribution of initiator and play type from play-by-play may misassign possessions, especially in partial-possession or defensive matchup data.

design.estimand: Within-case difference in usage gain between the top-ranked candidate teammate under one pre-specified profile definition and the other candidates, averaged over absence cases, for the absent player's primary play types.
design.unit: Absence case (one absent player and one team-season episode), with spells nested inside it; the case is the unit of inference.
design.sample: Minimum viable test: all 11 cases, with one primary profile definition pre-registered (for example, pre-absence initiation-rate similarity over a fixed pre-window). Spells are retained only for descriptive display.
design.power: Not adequate: with 11 cases, only very large hit-rate differences are detectable. The power calculation must be done before any analysis and will likely show the test is underpowered; the design should be reported as exploratory if it cannot reach the planned threshold.
design.controls: Measure profile and gains over non-overlapping pre- and post-absence windows; control for minutes, starter status, and same-position status as covariates or baseline comparators; use a minutes-only baseline ranking; exclude any window that overlaps the absence boundary; cap or exclude low-count play-type cells.
design.falsification: Pre-specify that the hypothesis is false if the closest-profile teammate is not the largest gainer in at least the pre-specified proportion of cases, and that a minutes-only baseline matches or beats the profile ranking.
design.multiplicity: Single pre-registered primary definition of closest profile and a single primary play-type set; other definitions reported as secondary with correction (for example Holm across definitions and play types).
design.decision_rule: Support requires the pre-registered profile ranking to beat the minutes-only baseline with a case-level interval excluding zero and a pre-set hit-rate threshold; otherwise report as uncertain or rejected. Any result that rests on post-absence windows is treated as artifact.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 through 2024-25 regular season and playoffs; 2025-26 regular season only after 2026-04-13 complete; 2025-26 playoffs only after 2026-06-21 complete; frozen at 2026-11-01.

What sample size and exposure is needed for absence-based usage redistribution tests?
How should regression to the mean and selection of absence spells be handled?
Which label and leakage risks arise when play-type initiation is derived from play-by-play outcomes?

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

messages.content:
Research question (as posed on 2026-11-01, in the area of player absence and offensive reorganization):
The teammate with the closest pre-absence initiation profile (or most minutes / initiations / same-position minutes) is the largest gainer in the absent player's primary types.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): n=148; 148 spells; 11 cases

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.
